description: Why we set goals in sport and how the SMART principle is applied to improve performance.
content_html:
Why Goal Setting Matters in Sport

Elite and recreational athletes alike use goal setting to direct effort and track progress. Without a clearly defined target, training can feel purposeless — athletes may work hard without knowing exactly what they are working towards. OCR identifies three distinct purposes for goal setting: to support exercise and training adherence, to motivate performers, and to improve and optimise performance. These three purposes are closely connected: a well-set goal keeps the athlete coming back to training (adherence), gives them a reason to push harder (motivation), and provides the framework for progressive development (performance improvement).

Goal Setting for Adherence

One of the most significant challenges in sport and physical activity is getting people to stick to training over time. Dropout rates are high, particularly among young people and those new to a sport. Goal setting reduces dropout by giving training a clear direction. When an athlete knows they are working towards a specific target — shaving two seconds off their 400 m personal best, increasing their maximum push-ups from 15 to 25 by the end of term — each session has a purpose. That sense of progress and purpose is a powerful driver of continued participation. Without it, training can feel like pointless repetition.

Goal Setting to Motivate

Goals provide the emotional fuel that drives a performer through demanding sessions. Knowing that a target is within reach — but requires consistent effort — keeps motivation high across a training programme. The target also provides a reference point for measuring effort: if you can see the gap closing between where you are now and where you want to be, each training session feels worthwhile. Kelly Holmes is a well-cited example of an athlete who used goals to maintain intense motivation through years of injury setbacks; her clarity about her Olympic 800 m and 1500 m targets helped sustain commitment through periods when the outcome felt distant.

Goal Setting to Improve Performance

Performance improvement requires structure. A goal provides the benchmark from which progress is measured and the endpoint towards which training is designed. Coaches use goals to plan progressive overload: if a cyclist aims to hold 280 watts for 20 minutes by the end of an eight-week block, each week’s sessions can be calibrated against that target. Without the goal, training lacks direction and improvement tends to plateau. The goal also sharpens the focus of the performer during sessions — they know which aspect of performance they are developing and why.

Key Fact

OCR identifies three purposes of goal setting: (1) to support exercise/training adherence — keeping athletes engaged and returning to training; (2) to motivate performers by giving them a reference point for progress; (3) to improve and optimise performance by providing a structured target for progressive development.

The SMART Principle

A goal is only useful if it is well-constructed. Vague intentions such as “get fitter” or “play better” provide no actionable direction. The SMART framework turns vague intentions into specific, trackable targets. In OCR Physical Education, SMART stands for: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Recorded and Timed. Note carefully that OCR uses “Achievable” and “Recorded” — these are different from other variants of the acronym used by other examination boards.

Breaking Down SMART

Specific: the target must state clearly what is to be achieved. “Get better at swimming” is not specific. “Reduce my 100 m freestyle time from 75 seconds to 70 seconds by the end of the half-term” is specific. A specific goal focuses training effort on exactly the right area and removes confusion about what success looks like.

Measurable: progress must be trackable using objective data. Times, distances, repetition counts, percentage success rates and scores all provide measurable evidence of progress. Without a measurable element, the performer cannot objectively determine whether they are improving or standing still.

Achievable: the goal must be within reach given the performer’s current ability, available training time and circumstances. A target that is too easy provides no motivational challenge. A target that is clearly impossible leads to frustration and demotivation. The ideal SMART target stretches the performer just beyond their current level — demanding real effort but attainable with consistent work. A county-level 400 m runner setting a target of running 44 seconds — a world-class standard — within six weeks would be setting an unachievable goal; targeting a two-second improvement on their current personal best is achievable.

Recorded: the goal must be written down and documented. Recording the goal creates accountability — both the performer and their coach can return to it, check progress and adjust the training plan if needed. An unrecorded goal exists only in memory, where it can be forgotten, altered unconsciously or abandoned without consequence. Recording also makes the goal real: when a young athlete writes down “I will achieve 15 press-ups in a set by the end of this month”, they are making a commitment that can be reviewed and celebrated or revised.

Timed: every SMART goal needs a deadline. “Improve my conversion rate to 60% by the end of the season” has a timed element; “improve my conversion rate eventually” does not. A deadline creates urgency, allows coaches to plan a progressive training schedule and provides a natural review point at which the goal can be evaluated and the next target set.

Different examination boards use slightly different versions of the SMART acronym. OCR’s version is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Recorded, Timed. The critical differences are the A and the R. Some boards use “Accepted” for A (meaning the goal is agreed with the coach) — OCR uses “Achievable” (meaning the goal is within reach). Some boards use “Realistic” for R — OCR uses “Recorded” (meaning the goal is documented). Writing the wrong letters in an OCR exam will cost marks on definition questions. Drill the exact five words: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Recorded, Timed. The A and the R are the exam traps.

Key Fact

OCR’s SMART = Specific (clearly defined), Measurable (trackable with data), Achievable (challenging but realistic), Recorded (written down and monitored), Timed (has a clear deadline). Learn these five exact words — not “Accepted” or “Realistic”, which are used by other boards.

Imagine a 15-year-old club sprinter whose current 100 m personal best is 12.8 seconds. A SMART target might be:

“Reduce my 100 m personal best from 12.8 seconds to 12.4 seconds (specific, measurable) within the next 10 weeks of structured sprint training (timed). An improvement of 0.4 seconds is achievable given my current fitness trajectory and twice-weekly coaching sessions (achievable). This target is written in my training log and reviewed with my coach after each weekly time trial (recorded).”

Every element of SMART is present. The recorded element is demonstrated by the training log entry and the regular coach review. The timed element gives both performer and coach a clear endpoint from which to work back and plan each week’s sessions.
exam_tip_html: On 6-mark analyse questions about goal setting, a common error is listing the five SMART letters without explaining what each means or applying each to a sporting scenario. To reach the higher marks, link each SMART element to a named example: e.g. “the goal is measurable because the athlete tracks their 100 m time each week with a stopwatch — objective data shows whether progress is being made.” On 3-mark describe or 4-mark explain questions, always use the OCR-specific letters — Achievable and Recorded — not ‘Accepted’ or ‘Realistic’, which belong to other boards’ specifications and will not be credited as definition answers in an OCR context. On the 1-mark identify question, remember the three purposes: adherence, motivation, and performance improvement — any one of these earns the mark but the answer must be precise enough to be one of these three concepts.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Goal setting has three purposes in OCR PE: to support exercise and training adherence, to motivate performers, and to improve and optimise performance.
  • SMART targets must be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Recorded and Timed — OCR uses ‘Achievable’ and ‘Recorded’, not the variants used by other boards.
  • A recorded goal is one that is written down and tracked over time, creating accountability for both the performer and the coach.

practice_questions.text: Identify one reason why an athlete would use goal setting during a training programme.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of the following: to support exercise/training adherence (keep the athlete returning to training consistently) (1); to motivate the performer by giving them a reference point for progress (1); to improve and/or optimise performance by providing a structured target (1). Do not credit vague answers such as 'to help them train' without specifying which of the three purposes.

practice_questions.text: State two features of a SMART target that help a performer track their progress.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct features: measurable — progress can be tracked using objective data such as times or distances (1); recorded — the goal is written down so it can be reviewed and monitored over time (1); timed — a deadline provides a natural review point (1). Maximum 2 marks; do not credit the same idea twice with different wording.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a SMART target in physical education.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correctly named and briefly explained element, up to 3 marks. Accept any three of: Specific — the goal is precisely defined with no ambiguity (1); Measurable — progress can be tracked using numbers or objective data (1); Achievable — the goal is challenging but realistic given the performer's current ability (1); Recorded — the goal is written down and documented for monitoring (1); Timed — the goal has a clear deadline (1). The letter A in OCR SMART stands for Achievable and R for Recorded — credit these terms or correct descriptions.

practice_questions.text: A club hockey player has written the following goal: 'Improve at hockey this season.' Explain why this goal does not meet the SMART criteria, and rewrite it as a SMART target.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for the critique: the goal is not specific — it does not state which aspect of hockey performance is to be improved (1); it is not measurable — there is no objective data to track whether improvement has occurred (1); it is not timed — no deadline is given (1); it is not recorded as a formal target (1). Maximum 2 for the critique. Up to 2 marks for the rewrite: a rewritten goal that includes a specific and measurable element (e.g. 'increase my penalty corner conversion rate from 30% to 45%') (1); and at least two further SMART elements (achievable context, recorded in training log, timed deadline) (1). Accept valid alternative sport-specific targets.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a county-level badminton player could use the SMART principle to set a goal that supports both their motivation and their long-term performance improvement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses all five SMART elements with explanation of each linked to both motivation and performance improvement in a badminton context. Points might include: Specific — 'increase first-serve accuracy to 70%' gives the player a precise focus for training, directing effort to the right technical area (1); Measurable — recording first-serve percentages each session shows the gap closing, which itself motivates by demonstrating progress (1); Achievable — a realistic target prevents demotivation from repeated failure; an unachievable target would reduce training adherence (1); Recorded — logging the goal and weekly measurements creates accountability and a narrative of progress (1); Timed — 'by the county championships in 8 weeks' creates urgency, allows the coach to structure progressive weekly drills (1). Strong responses link each element to both motivation and performance improvement explicitly, rather than treating them as separate. May note that the recorded element also helps the coach adapt sessions if progress stalls.

Secure: At least four SMART elements explained with mostly accurate links to the badminton context. Mentions both motivation and performance but may not connect them consistently.

Developing: Names at least three SMART elements with some explanation. Limited link to motivation or performance improvement. May simply list without analysing.

Emerging: Names SMART letters without explaining them; little or no sporting application.

practice_questions.text: Write a full SMART target for a 16-year-old club javelin thrower whose current personal best is 31 metres, preparing for the county championship in nine weeks.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a specific and measurable element: e.g. 'throw a minimum of 35 metres' — a named distance improvement at the named event (1). 1 mark for the achievable element with context: a 4-metre improvement in nine weeks is achievable for a county-level athlete with twice-weekly coaching sessions (1). 1 mark for timed and recorded: 'by the county championship in 9 weeks, recorded in training log and reviewed weekly with the coach' (1). Accept alternative distances or timelines provided they are internally consistent. Do not credit 'Accepted' or 'Realistic' as the OCR terms for A and R.

knowledge_checks.q: According to OCR, which of the following is NOT one of the three purposes of goal setting?
In OCR's SMART target framework, what does the letter 'R' stand for?
In OCR's SMART target framework, what does the letter 'A' stand for?
A SMART target must be _____, meaning progress can be tracked using times, distances or other objective data.
Match each SMART element to its correct meaning:
right: Has a clear deadline creating urgency and a review point
Precisely defines what is to be achieved
Written down and monitored so progress can be tracked

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three purposes of goal setting according to OCR?
flashcard_questions.a: Exercise/training adherence, motivation, and improving/optimising performance.

flashcard_questions.q: What does SMART stand for in OCR Physical Education?
What does 'specific' mean in a SMART target?
flashcard_questions.a: The goal is precisely defined with no ambiguity about what is to be achieved.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'measurable' mean in a SMART target?
flashcard_questions.a: Progress can be tracked using times, distances or other objective data.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'achievable' mean in a SMART target (OCR)?
flashcard_questions.a: The goal is challenging but realistic given the performer's current ability.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'recorded' mean in a SMART target (OCR)?
flashcard_questions.a: The goal is written down and documented so it can be monitored and reviewed.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'timed' mean in a SMART target?
flashcard_questions.a: The goal has a clear deadline, creating urgency and a natural review point.

flashcard_questions.q: What is training adherence in the context of goal setting?
flashcard_questions.a: Continuing to take part in exercise or training consistently rather than dropping out.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does goal setting support training adherence?
flashcard_questions.a: It gives each session a clear purpose, so training feels worthwhile rather than pointless.

flashcard_questions.q: What exam trap exists with OCR's SMART acronym?
flashcard_questions.a: A = Achievable and R = Recorded (not 'Accepted' or 'Realistic' used by other boards).

flashcard_questions.q: Why must a SMART goal be 'achievable'?
flashcard_questions.a: A target too easy gives no challenge; one too hard leads to frustration and dropout.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must a SMART goal be 'recorded'?
flashcard_questions.a: Recording creates accountability and allows both performer and coach to track progress.

glossary_terms.definition: Continuing to take part in exercise or training consistently over time, rather than dropping out.
The quality of a SMART target being precisely defined with no ambiguity about what is to be achieved.
The quality of a SMART target that can be tracked using a number, time, distance or other objective measure.
The quality of a SMART target being challenging enough to motivate but realistic given the performer's current ability and circumstances.
The quality of a SMART target being written down and tracked so that progress can be monitored and reviewed over time.
The quality of a SMART target having a clear deadline by which the goal should be achieved, creating urgency and a review point.
A goal-setting framework where targets are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Recorded and Timed.

hero_image_caption: Goal setting gives athletes direction, motivation and a framework for measuring progress.
